claims.text: The initial material is an as-cast, single-phase equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy.
WTaTiVZr is a refractory high-entropy alloy.
WTaTiVZr has enhanced high-temperature plastic strain relative to pure tungsten.
WTaTiVZr has enhanced high-temperature toughness relative to pure tungsten.
Atomic-size mismatches among the refractory elements generate local lattice distortions and stress fields in WTaTiVZr.
Local lattice distortions reduce the energetic barrier for deformation-twin nucleation during high-temperature loading.
Local lattice distortions promote dislocation cross-slip in WTaTiVZr.
Deformation twins can hinder dislocation motion and generate strain hardening.
Intersecting twin boundaries can enable rapid dislocation motion and cross-slip, producing more homogeneous plastic deformation.
Twin-dislocation interactions in WTaTiVZr enhance toughness and delay crack propagation.
Pure tungsten deforms primarily through dislocation-mediated mechanisms and has limited or absent nano-twinning under the proposed conditions.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit a lower apparent creep stress exponent than pure tungsten.
WTaTiVZr will contain more nano-twins than pure tungsten after identical high-temperature loading.
WTaTiVZr will show enhanced dislocation mobility relative to pure tungsten.
Nanoindentation creep of TaTiVWZr has previously been evaluated at elevated temperature and compared with pure tungsten using stress exponent, activation volume, and activation energy.
The proposed twinning mechanism is active only at high temperatures relevant to plasma-facing-component service.
At lower temperatures, the driving force for nano-twin formation may be insufficient and other deformation mechanisms may dominate.
Identically conditioned high-temperature tests of WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten are proposed as the controlled comparison.
Failure to observe statistically significant increases in plastic strain, fracture toughness, nano-twinning, or cross-slip in WTaTiVZr relative to pure tungsten would falsify the hypothesis.
